strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored failure mode: VLMs defaulting to memorized 'internet-prior' answers over actual pixel-level visual evidence, using neutral (non-leading) prompts and genuinely modified images rather than biased text cues, which improves on prior benchmarks like PhD-ccs/VLind-Bench/HallusionBench.

Very broad and systematic benchmark: 7 diverse domains (animals, logos, flags, chess pieces, board games, optical illusions, novel patterned grids), ~1,400+ images at 3 resolutions, with a largely automated LLM+diffusion-model generation pipeline plus manual QC, making the resource substantial and (with code/data release) potentially reusable.

Strong internal controls that support the causal claim of bias: a 'sanity check' showing all 5 models score 100% on identification/counting for unmodified images, which sharply contrasts with near-floor accuracy on counterfactual images and rules out the possibility that the counting task itself is inherently too hard.

Comprehensive set of follow-up analyses beyond the core result: resolution variation, adversarial in-image text naming the subject (further hurting accuracy), Y/N identification (Q3) confirming the same bias, and prompting interventions (debiasing, double-check) that only marginally help — jointly making a convincing case that the bias is deep-seated rather than an artifact of prompt design.

The patterned-grid task (Task 7), which contains no real-world prior knowledge at all, is a clever control showing that even purely local pattern-completion bias (not internet memorization per se) can override direct visual counting, broadening the significance of the finding.
Extensive, well-organized appendix with full task design, prompts, ground-truth computation, and qualitative examples, aiding reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: No human baseline/calibration is reported for the counting tasks themselves (e.g., counting stripes on a small logo or pieces on a chessboard at given resolutions); while the sanity check on unmodified images is a reasonable proxy, a direct human accuracy comparison on the counterfactual images would more rigorously separate 'bias override' from 'genuine perceptual difficulty of subtle edits.'

Only five models are tested, all proprietary and accessed via API (Gemini-2.5 Pro, Sonnet-3.7, GPT-4.1, o3, o4-mini); no open-source/open-weight VLMs (e.g., LLaVA, Qwen-VL, InternVL) are evaluated despite being discussed in the intro/related work, limiting generality of conclusions and reproducibility by the broader community.

Results appear to be based on single runs per item at temperature=1.0 with no repeated trials, variance/confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing, which is a concern given nontrivial sampling temperature and could affect the reliability of fine-grained accuracy comparisons across models/tasks.

The core phenomenon (VLMs relying on language/vision priors over image content) is already documented in prior bias/hallucination literature (e.g., HallusionBench, VLind-Bench, PhD); the contribution is primarily a broader, more carefully controlled benchmark rather than a fundamentally new insight or a proposed mitigation, somewhat limiting novelty.

The image-generation pipeline itself relies on VLMs/diffusion models (Gemini-2.0 Flash, GPT-4o) which the authors acknowledge have their own biases, potentially introducing subtle confounds or artifacts into the counterfactual images that are only caught by manual review rather than systematic validation.

No proposed mitigation or deeper mechanistic analysis (e.g., probing vision encoder representations, as speculated in the discussion) is carried out, leaving the paper primarily diagnostic; the practical takeaway for building less-biased VLMs remains limited beyond 'current prompting fixes barely help.'

strengths: Introduces VLMBias, a large-scale (1,392 core images, up to 4,176 with extensions) benchmark spanning 7 diverse domains (animals, logos, flags, chess pieces, game boards, optical illusions, patterned grids), generated via a careful, largely automated pipeline with human quality control.

Methodologically well-motivated design choice of using neutral prompts with counterfactual images and objective counting questions, addressing genuine limitations (biased prompt wording, Y/N-only tasks, small scale) of prior VLM-bias benchmarks (PhD-ccs, VLind-Bench, ViLP, HallusionBench), with a clear comparison table justifying the contribution.

Extremely thorough experimental program: sanity checks confirming models recognize unmodified subjects (100% accuracy) before testing on counterfactuals; linear probing of vision encoders showing visual features are sufficient (95%) even though end-to-end VLM accuracy is not, isolating the bias to the language/decision stage rather than perception; background removal ablation showing large accuracy gains; resolution robustness checks; multi-run reliability/consistency and confidence analysis; adversarial in-image text; few-shot/debiasing/double-check prompting; reasoning-length vs. accuracy analysis (overthinking phenomenon); cross-model-family checks to rule out generation-evaluation bias; evaluation of newer models (GPT-5, Grok-4) and open-source/pointing-specialized models (Moondream, Molmo).

Includes a human subject study (78 participants, time-limited viewing) providing a compelling baseline showing humans vastly outperform VLMs even under severe time pressure, supporting that the counterfactual images are not inherently ambiguous.
Results are consistent and clearly presented across many tables/figures, and qualitative examples (e.g., few-shot distrust behavior) add valuable insight into failure modes.
Very thorough appendix documenting data generation pipelines, prompts, and quality control for every task, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central finding—that VLMs over-rely on memorized/prior knowledge rather than fine-grained visual evidence—echoes existing literature (e.g., 'VLMs are Blind', visual hallucination and language-prior studies), so the conceptual novelty is more about the benchmark/methodology than the underlying scientific insight.

The benchmark focuses almost exclusively on counting-style tasks; while this is well justified, it narrows the claim of general 'bias' to a fairly specific failure mode (fine-grained enumeration under salient prior expectations), and the title/framing ('Vision Language Models are Biased') may overstate generality relative to the counting-centric evidence.
The extensive human study is conducted only on the animal-leg-counting subtask, not across all 7 domains, limiting how broadly the human-vs-model comparison generalizes.

Image generation/editing relies on the same class of generative models being evaluated in one domain (though the paper does attempt to control for this via cross-family checks), and subtle generation artifacts (e.g., unnatural leg placement) could occasionally confound difficulty vs. bias explanations.

Statistical robustness checks (5-run consistency) are only performed for 2 of the 5 main models, and formal significance testing/error bars are largely absent throughout the many reported percentages.

Some of the many sub-analyses (e.g., resolution, tool-use, few-shot) are somewhat exploratory and not always tied to a single coherent hypothesis, making the paper's contribution feel like a large collection of related but loosely unified findings rather than a tightly focused study.
